title: II. Lyagavy
paragraphs: So he had to travel fast, and he had no money for horses. All he had was forty kopecks, all that was left after so many years of prosperity! But at home he had an old silver watch that had stopped working long ago. He grabbed it and took it to a Jewish watchmaker with a shop in the market-place. The man gave him six roubles for it.

“And I never expected that!” cried Mitya, ecstatic. (He was still in a state of ecstasy.) He seized his six roubles and ran home. There he borrowed three roubles from the people of the house. They were so fond of him that they handed it over gladly, though it was all they had. In his excitement Mitya told them right then that his fate would be decided that day. In desperate haste he described the whole scheme he had put to Samsonov, how Samsonov had decided, what he himself hoped for the future, and so on. These people had been told many of their lodger’s secrets before, so they saw him as a gentleman with no pride at all, almost one of themselves. Now that he had nine roubles, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to the Volovya station. This is how it came to be remembered and put on record that “at midday, on the day before the event, Mitya had not a farthing, and that he had sold his watch to get money and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in the presence of witnesses.”
I note this fact now. Later it will be clear why I do.

He was radiant with joyful hope that at last he would solve all his difficulties. Yet as he came near Volovya station, he shook at the thought of what Grushenka might be doing while he was gone. What if she decided today to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch? That was why he had left without telling her, and why he had ordered his landlady not to say where he had gone if anyone came asking for him.

“I must get back tonight, I must,” he kept saying as the cart jolted along. “And I expect I’ll have to bring this Lyagavy back here with me ... to draw up the deed.” So Mitya mused, his heart pounding. But alas! His dreams were not fated to come true.

First, he was late. He took a short cut from Volovya station, and it turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, the priest was not at home in Ilyinskoe. He had gone off to a neighboring village. As Mitya set out there with the same worn-out horses and looked for him, it was almost dark.

The priest was a shy, pleasant-looking little man. He told Mitya right away that Lyagavy had stayed with him at first but was now at Suhoy Possyolok, spending the night in the forester’s cottage, because he was buying timber there too. Mitya begged him urgently to take him to Lyagavy at once and so “save him, so to speak.” After some hesitation the priest agreed to guide him to Suhoy Possyolok. His curiosity was plainly aroused. But unluckily he proposed going on foot, since it was not “much over” a verst. Mitya agreed, naturally, and set off with his yard-long strides, so that the poor priest nearly had to run to keep up. He was a very cautious man, though not old.

Mitya started talking to him about his plans too. Nervous and excited, he asked for advice about Lyagavy and talked the whole way. The priest listened closely but gave little advice. He fended off Mitya’s questions with: “I don’t know. Ah, I can’t say. How can I tell?” and so on. When Mitya began to speak about his quarrel with his father over the inheritance, the priest was truly alarmed, because he depended on Fyodor Pavlovitch in some way. He did ask, in surprise, why Mitya called the peasant-trader Gorstkin by the name Lyagavy. Then he explained, helpfully, that the man’s name really was Lyagavy, but nobody called him that, since the name would badly offend him. Mitya must be sure to call him Gorstkin, “or you’ll do nothing with him; he won’t even listen to you,” the priest finished.

For a moment Mitya was a little taken aback. He said that Samsonov had called him that. When he heard this, the priest let the subject drop. He would have done well to say aloud what he doubted: if Samsonov had sent Mitya to that peasant and called him Lyagavy, was there something wrong in it? Was Samsonov making a fool of him? But Mitya had no time to stop over trifles like that. He hurried on, striding. Only when he reached Suhoy Possyolok did he see that they had come not one verst, or one and a half, but at least three. That annoyed him, but he kept himself under control.

They went into the hut. The forester lived in one half, and Gorstkin was staying in the other half, the better room, on the far side of the passage. They went into that room and lit a tallow candle. The hut was stiflingly hot. On the table stood a samovar that had gone cold, a tray of cups, an empty rum bottle, a half-full bottle of vodka, and some half-eaten crusts of wheaten bread. The visitor himself lay at full length on the bench, with his coat bunched up under his head for a pillow, snoring heavily. Mitya stood there at a loss.

“Of course I have to wake him. My business is too important. I came in such a hurry. I need to get back today,” he said, very agitated. But the priest and the forester stood silent and offered no opinion. Mitya went over and tried to wake the man himself. He tried hard, but the sleeper did not wake.

“He’s drunk,” Mitya decided. “Good Lord! What do I do? What do I do?” Terribly impatient, he started tugging him by the arms and the legs, shaking his head, hauling him up and sitting him on the bench. But after long effort, all he got out of the drunken man was silly grunts and violent, slurred oaths.
“No, you’d better wait a while,” the priest said at last. “He’s obviously in no state for it.”
“He’s been drinking all day,” the forester put in.
“Good heavens!” cried Mitya. “If only you knew how much this matters to me, and how desperate I am!”
“No, you’d better wait till morning,” the priest said again.
“Till morning? Mercy! That’s impossible!”
And in his despair he was about to go at the sleeping man again, but he stopped at once, seeing how useless it was. The priest said nothing, and the sleepy forester looked sullen.

“What terrible tragedies real life cooks up for people,” said Mitya, in utter despair. Sweat was pouring down his face. The priest used the moment to point out, quite sensibly, that even if Mitya did manage to wake the man, he would still be drunk and unable to talk. “And your business is important,” he said, “so you’d certainly do better to put it off till morning.” With a hopeless gesture, Mitya gave in.

“Father, I will stay here with a light, and seize the favorable moment. The minute he wakes I’ll begin. I’ll pay you for the light,” he said to the forester, “and for the night’s lodging too. You’ll remember Dmitri Karamazov. Only, Father, I don’t know what we’ll do with you. Where will you sleep?”
“No, I’m going home. I’ll take his horse and ride home,” he said, pointing to the forester. “And now I’ll say good-bye. I wish you every success.”

So that was settled. The priest rode off on the forester’s horse, glad to get away. Still, he shook his head uneasily, wondering if he ought to tell his benefactor Fyodor Pavlovitch about this strange business the next day, “or he may hear of it at an unlucky moment, get angry, and take back his favor.”

The forester scratched himself, went back to his room without a word, and Mitya sat down on the bench to “catch the favorable moment,” as he put it. A deep gloom hung over his soul like a heavy fog. A profound, bitter gloom! He sat and thought, but could come to no conclusion. The candle burned low, a cricket chirped, and the hot room grew more and more stifling. All at once he pictured the garden, the path behind the garden, the door of his father’s house mysteriously opening and Grushenka running in. He jumped up from the bench.

“It’s a tragedy!” he said, grinding his teeth. Mechanically he walked over to the sleeping man and looked into his face. He was a lean, middle-aged peasant with a very long face, flaxen curls, and a long, thin, reddish beard. He wore a blue cotton shirt and a black waistcoat, and the chain of a silver watch showed from its pocket. Mitya looked into that face with fierce hatred, and for some reason he could not name, the curly hair annoyed him most of all.

What was so unbearably humiliating was this. He had left matters of great importance and made great sacrifices, and now here he was, Mitya, utterly exhausted, with business of such urgency, standing over this blockhead on whom his whole fate hung. And the blockhead snored away as if nothing were wrong, as if he had dropped from another planet.

“Oh, the irony of fate!” cried Mitya. Quite losing his head, he went back to shaking the tipsy peasant awake. He did it with a kind of fury. He pulled at him, shoved him, even hit him. But after five minutes of wasted effort, he went back to his bench in helpless despair and sat down.

“Stupid! Stupid!” cried Mitya. “And how dishonorable all this is!” something made him add. His head began to ache horribly. “Should he throw it all up and leave for good?” he wondered. “No, wait till tomorrow now. I’ll stay on purpose. What else did I come for? Besides, I have no way to leave. How am I to get away from here now? Oh, the idiocy of it!”

But his head ached more and more. He sat without moving, and without meaning to he dozed off and fell asleep sitting there. He seemed to have slept two hours or more. What woke him was a headache so unbearable that he could have screamed. His temples were hammering and the top of his head throbbed. It was a long time before he was properly awake and understood what had happened to him.

At last he saw that the room was full of charcoal fumes from the stove, and that he might suffocate. And the drunken peasant lay there snoring still. The candle was guttering and about to go out. Mitya cried out and ran, staggering, across the passage into the forester’s room. The forester woke right away. But when he heard that the other room was full of fumes, he took it with strange unconcern, though he did go and see to it. This surprised and angered Mitya.
“But he’s dead, he’s dead! And ... what do I do then?” cried Mitya, frantic.

They threw open the doors and opened a window and the chimney. Mitya fetched a pail of water from the passage. First he soaked his own head. Then he found a rag, dipped it in the water, and laid it on Lyagavy’s head. The forester still treated the whole thing with contempt, and as he opened the window he said grumpily:
“It’ll be all right now.”

He went back to bed, leaving Mitya a lit lantern. Mitya fussed over the drunken peasant for half an hour, wetting his head, and solemnly vowed not to sleep all night. But he was so worn out that when he sat down for a moment to catch his breath, his eyes closed. Without meaning to, he stretched out full length on the bench and slept like the dead.

It was dreadfully late when he woke, somewhere around nine o’clock. The sun was shining brightly through the two small windows of the hut. The curly-headed peasant sat on the bench with his coat on. In front of him stood another samovar and another bottle. Yesterday’s bottle was finished, and the new one was more than half empty. Mitya jumped up and saw at once that the cursed peasant was drunk again, hopelessly and incurably. He stared at him for a moment, eyes wide. The peasant was watching him in silence, slyly, with insulting calm and even a kind of contemptuous condescension, or so Mitya thought. He rushed up to him.
“Excuse me, you see ... I ... the forester here has probably told you. I’m Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of the old Karamazov whose copse you’re buying.”
“That’s a lie!” said the peasant, calm and sure.
“A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“I don’t know any of your Fyodor Pavlovitches,” said the peasant, thick-tongued.

“You’re haggling with him over the copse, the copse! Do wake up, pull yourself together. Father Pavel from Ilyinskoe brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and he sent me to you,” Mitya gasped, out of breath.
“You’re l-lying!” Lyagavy blurted out again. Mitya’s legs went cold.
“For mercy’s sake! This is no joke! Maybe you’re drunk. Yet you can talk and understand ... or else ... I understand nothing!”
“You’re a painter!”
“For mercy’s sake! I’m Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov. I have an offer for you, a good offer ... a very good offer, about the copse!”
The peasant stroked his beard with great importance.
“No, you took on the job and turned out a scamp. You’re a scoundrel!”
“I tell you, you’re mistaken,” cried Mitya, wringing his hands in despair. The peasant went on stroking his beard, then suddenly narrowed his eyes slyly.
“No, you show me this: name me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand that?”

Mitya stepped back gloomily, and suddenly “something seemed to hit him on the head,” as he said afterwards. In an instant a light seemed to break in his mind, “a light was kindled and I grasped it all.” He stood there stunned. How could he, a man of intelligence after all, have fallen for such folly, been drawn into such an adventure, and kept it up for almost twenty-four hours, fussing around this Lyagavy and wetting his head?
“Why, the man’s drunk, dead drunk, and he’ll go on drinking for a week now. What’s the use of waiting here? And what if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What if she—? Oh, God, what have I done?”

The peasant sat watching him and grinning. At another time Mitya might have killed the fool in a rage, but now he felt as weak as a child. He walked quietly to the bench, picked up his overcoat, put it on without a word, and left the hut. The forester was not in the next room. There was nobody there. He took fifty kopecks in small change from his pocket and left them on the table for his night’s lodging, the candle, and the trouble he had caused. Outside the hut he saw nothing but forest on every side. He walked at random, not knowing whether to turn right or left. Hurrying there the evening before with the priest, he had not noticed the road. In his heart he felt no wish for revenge on anyone, not even Samsonov. He strode along a narrow forest path, aimless and dazed, paying no attention to where he was going. A child could have knocked him down, he was so weak in body and soul. Somehow he got out of the forest, however, and a view of fields, bare after the harvest, opened out as far as the eye could see.
“What despair! What death all around!” he repeated, striding on and on.

He was saved by meeting an old merchant who was being driven across country in a hired trap. Mitya caught up with him and asked the way, and it turned out that the old merchant was also going to Volovya. After some talk Mitya climbed into the trap. Three hours later they arrived. At Volovya, Mitya immediately ordered posting-horses for the drive to town, and suddenly realized he was ravenously hungry. While the horses were being harnessed, they made him an omelette. He ate it all in a moment, ate a huge hunk of bread, ate a sausage, and drank three glasses of vodka. After eating, his spirits and his heart grew lighter. He flew toward town, urged the driver on, and suddenly came up with a new and “unalterable” plan to get that “accursed money” before evening. “And to think, only to think that a man’s life should be ruined for the sake of that paltry three thousand!” he cried, scornfully. “I’ll settle it today.” And if it had not been for the thought of Grushenka and of what might have happened to her, which never left him, he might have become quite cheerful again.... But the thought of her stabbed him to the heart every moment, like a sharp knife.
At last they arrived, and Mitya ran straight to Grushenka.
